title: Embodied Representations
excerpt: Biological representations are fundamentally embodied and action-oriented; the prime directive of the brain is to map sensory input to control outputs Body schemas The brain encodes a "body schema" through somatotopic maps in primary sensory and motor cortices
html:
Biological representations are fundamentally embodied and action-oriented; the prime directive of the brain is to map sensory input to control outputs

Body schemas

The brain encodes a "body schema" through somatotopic maps in primary sensory and motor cortices. Classic studies by Penfield revealed an orderly "homunculus" mapping of the body on these cortices, with body parts that have finer sensation or require dexterity (e.g. fingers) occupying disproportionately large cortical areas 1. These maps are plastic and update with experience or injury. A 2025 human study maps connections between vision and touch (Figure) 5. The study maps body-related representations in visual cortex (Figure).

A preserved latent manifold supports wrist, reach-to-grasp, and motor imagery, implying that new skills repurpose existing "neural modes" rather than invent new ones 2 A monkey study examines arm-movement representations (Figure) 6. The study compares movement speed with neural trajectories (Figure).

Forward models

The motor system constantly generates internal predictions of sensory outcomes for planned movements. The cerebellum and associated circuits are thought to implement forward models that transform motor commands into fine-grained expected sensory feedback 3, which can be contrasted with actual outcomes during learning (more on this later). A striking example is our inability to tickle ourselves: when you attempt to self-tickle, the brain (via a copy of the motor command, an efference copy) predicts the tactile outcome and cancels it out 4

Image schemas

An image schema is a recurrent, dynamic sensorimotor pattern-things like containment (in/out), force dynamics (push/pull), paths (source-goal trajectories), and balance/equilibrium states-abstracted over thousands of episodes and later "re-used" by language and abstract thought. Lakoff & Johnson’s original philosophical formulation is now backed by fMRI and lesion data showing that reasoning about these patterns re-activates premotor, parietal and posterior-temporal regions that code underlying actions and spatial relations

Within  150 ms of viewing a potential action-scenario the dorsal fronto-parietal network instantiates containment, path or force dynamics as low-dimensional manifolds that feed forward to prefrontal and temporal cortices where they scaffold semantic and linguistic inferences.

The brain seems to use them as a layer between low-level kinematics and high-level symbolic reasoning, placing them in the hierarchical region where mid-level action representations (e.g "move arm to mug handle" or "jump into the water") reside

Embodied semantics

Abstract or high-level cognitive representations, like language and concepts, show evidence of sensorimotor grounding in the brain. According to the embodied cognition view, understanding a concept or word involves partial re-activation of the sensory and motor circuits associated with that concept. Empirical studies support this: for example, reading action verbs like "kick," "pick," or "lick" preferentially activates motor cortex regions corresponding to feet, hands, or mouth respectively - mirroring the body part used in the described action

Similarly, brain imaging has shown that thinking about or listening to descriptions of, say, the taste of cinnamon can engage olfactory and gustatory regions, or hearing a sentence about a texture can engage somatosensory areas. Moreover, transiently disrupting motor cortex with magnetic stimulation can selectively impair people’s understanding of action-related words, suggesting those motor circuits contribute functionally to language comprehension. These findings indicate that the brain’s semantic representations are not amodal symbols but are grounded in modality-specific systems.

General intelligence and parietal affordance maps

Affordance maps

In macaques and humans, single-unit, LFP, and fMRI work all converge on the idea that posterior parietal cortex (PPC) does not passively list the world’s contents-it maps how the body could interact with what is out there. Area V6A, for example, dynamically recodes a graspable object as soon as it becomes the goal of an arm movement; nearly half of the neurons flip their firing depending on whether the animal will reach, grasp, or merely look, even when the retinal image is unchanged. That "visual-for-action" code persists through movement execution and is updated online by proprioceptive error, giving PPC the flavour of a forward state-estimator tuned for affordances rather than for neutral object identity.

The same dorsal codes feed forward into prefrontal regions that maintain, rank and inhibit candidate actions.

Overlap with P-FIT theory and general intelligence measures

The Parieto-Frontal Integration Theory (P-FIT) argues that individual differences in general intelligence reflect the efficiency with which this fronto-parietal loop integrates perceptual evidence with candidate motor programs and evaluates them against task goals. A landmark meta-analysis found that Brodmann area 7 (superior parietal) was engaged in >70% of reasoning tasks and that dorsolateral PFC, anterior cingulate and angular gyrus co-activation explained roughly 40% of the variance in full-scale IQ across 37 neuroimaging studies. White-matter integrity of the superior longitudinal fasciculus-the main parietal-frontal highway-predicts fluid intelligence as robustly as grey-matter volume.

So the intraparietal sulcus and superior parietal lobule that correlate most strongly with IQ scores are exactly where the brain computes spatial transformations, object manipulability, and action sequences. When you’re solving Raven’s Progressive Matrices (the gold standard IQ test), you’re literally using the same neural machinery that computes "how do I grasp this object?" The parietal cortex is performing spatial rotations, transformation sequences, and relational mappings - whether you’re mentally rotating shapes on an IQ test or planning how to pick up a coffee cup.

Synthesis

Fluid reasoning may amount to running rapidly-refined internal motor simulations under executive control. Three lines of evidence reinforce this interpretation. First, mental-rotation, visuomotor imitation, and even matrix-reasoning tasks all recruit dorsal parietal voxels whose tuning curves look indistinguishable from those engaged by actual reach-to-grasp movements, suggesting that "spatial" reasoning recycles motor primitives. Second, disrupting these parietal sectors with TMS or lesion selectively impairs both tool-use kinematics and abstract reasoning scores, implying a shared causal substrate. Third, developmental expansions of BA 7/40 correlate with the emergence of complex tool use and the steepest gains in fluid intelligence across primate evolution, fitting Cisek’s "affordance-competition" framework in which ever-richer action repertoires drive selection for larger fronto-parietal loops.

Assuming a definition of intelligence as one’s ability to produce predictive models, the centrality of affordance-computing parietal regions in general human intelligence suggests that the human ability to model and manipulate the environment is fundamentally based on representations of potential actions and their consequences; this form of learning and representation is fundamentally distinct from leading A.I training recipes

This convergence suggests that abstract reasoning emerges from embodied spatial computation rather than being a separate "higher-order" process. The brain doesn’t have distinct systems for thinking versus acting - thinking IS a form of internalized action simulation. Even when you’re doing pure mathematics, you’re leveraging neural circuits evolved for navigating and manipulating the physical world.

Cortical population codes that evolved to predict the sensory consequences of candidate movements now serve as the proto-symbols that higher-order cognition manipulates. Contemporary AI systems that learn static embeddings from disembodied data streams are missing this affordance-first substrate; closing the gap will likely require models that keep an online, parietal-style action manifold tightly coupled to their perception and planning modules.

Neural recycling of spatial systems

Evolutionary co-option of navigational mechanisms (e.g grid cells and place cells) for representing non-spatial relationships and abstract knowledge

From an AGI engineering perspective, this suggests that spatial reasoning might be the fundamental substrate for all abstract cognition.

The key transferable principle is that abstract reasoning emerges from concrete spatial computation rather than being a separate higher-order process.
